items.title: 68003_Eddie Sauter oral history interview
items.q: That's why Sauter-Finegan came out the way it did.

ctx.x: an interview that you did with George Simon at the Metronome in '46, and this was right after you had been writing for Ray McKinley and I got a real sense of your being dissatisfied with having to write for "dance bands", having to keep a steady tempo, a steady meter.

Bill Finegan got the same thing. That's why Sauter-Finegan came out the way it did. You'd write a block, it was mainly for rhythm and not much else. You'd write a section this way, and the reason was it had a rhythmic touch to it. The way it was played made the difference. But you know, as you write, pretty soon you can't think of anything anymore, you're so limited.
